new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: rendered PDF page 13 of (printed p. 205, header 'HUASTECA NAHUATL 205') at 150 dpi and read it as an image. Second paragraph, immediately after the vowel-length paragraph and before the heading 'Major Phonological Processes', reads exactly: 'Stress is on the penultimate syllable except for a few rare exceptions. In these exceptions stress will be.' Verbatim as reported; the scanned excerpt matches. Printed p. 203 (PDF p. 11) confirms scope: 'Huasteca Nahuatl (HN) is spoken by 350,000 Indians.. San Luis Potosi, Hidalgo, Veracruz, and.. northern tip of Puebla', two dialects divided by a line 'from east of Platon Sanchez, Veracruz down to Tianguistengo, Hidalgo'; principal consult…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; the handful of words that deviate are marked with a written accent (none are listed in the phonology section). The same rule is stated for the same dialect in the Bellers' teaching course (Curso del náhuatl moderno vol. 1, p. 11: 'El acento prosódico.. recae sobre la penúltima sílaba aunque ésta termine en consonante'), and for the nch-area municipios specifically by Hernández Beatriz 2013, p. 15: 'La sílaba acentuada, en la mayoría de las veces, está en la penúltima sílaba de la palabra.. aunque por las variaciones dialectales se acentúa también como aguda.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Beller & Beller 1979 or Hernández Beatriz 2013. (Croft 1951, p. 33, on the Western/Matlapa dialect reports secondary stress on the first syllable of words of 3+ syllables; not re-read here.)
new_statements.exceptions: Beller & Beller: 'a few rare exceptions', to be written with an accent, not enumerated. Hernández Beatriz 2013, pp. 95-96 and 99 (Huasteca hidalguense): in the southern part of the region (Huejutla/Huazalingo side) some present-tense singular verbs ending in -i/-o are stressed on the final syllable because the final vowel is lost (mawiltí 'plays', maltí 'bathes', kitlatí 'burns it', ki'ilwí 'tells him', tlaneskí 'it dawned'), versus northern mawiltia, maltía etc; fn. 34: read with penultimate stress these forms become past tense. Spanish loans: agudas become graves, esdrújulas keep their stress (p. 52: teléfano, elikótero).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule for the whole 'Huasteca Nahuatl' language as the Bellers define it (E dialect = Huautla, Hgo; W = Tamazunchale, SLP), stated in a phonology section that ignores vowel length. Hernández Beatriz's statement is a word-level orthographic convention for the Huasteca hidalguense (nch municipios), based on elicited isolated words (vocabularios) across CONAFE localities.
new_statements.identity_note: No description is filed under nch itself: Glottolog lists no descriptive work (only Garcia 2014 dialectology MA and Stiles 1982 sociolinguistics), OLAC lists only four 2007 SIL literacy items and an AILLA deposit. The quoted statement is from Beller & Beller 1979, whose 'Huasteca Nahuatl' covers the whole Huasteca (350,000 speakers in SLP, Hidalgo, Veracruz, N Puebla) with an E dialect (principal consultant from Cuatenahuatl near Huautla, Hidalgo) and a W dialect (Tamazunchale, SLP); SIL/WALS/Glottolog file that sketch under nhe (east2538) / nhw (west2624), and the Huejutla-Huazalingo-Platón Sánchez zone later coded nch lies inside its stated coverage but had no consultant of its own. SIL's 2007 nch phrasebook (Aclaraciones, PDF p.4-5) defines the Central variety as Huejutla de Reyes, Huazalingo, San Felipe Orizatlán, Jaltocán (Hgo), Chalma, Platón Sánchez, Chiconamel (Ver.), San Martín Chalchicuautla, Tamazunchale (SLP), 'like Western except tl > t'. The nch-specific corroboration is Hernández Beatriz 2013 (UNAM licenciatura thesis on the Huasteca hidalguense: Orizatlán, Jaltocán, Huejutla, Huazalingo, Yahualica, Atlapexco, Huautla, Xochiatipan), p.15: penultimate stress 'en la mayoría de las veces', with dialectal final-stressed (aguda) forms; pp.95-96 attribute the aguda forms to loss of the final vowel in present-tense verbs in the southern part of the region (mawiltí ~ mawiltia). Kimball 1980's Huazalinguillo dialect (municipio Huazalingo, Hgo) also falls inside the nch area although Glottolog/Grambank file it under west2624.
